_about: Viva regression answers for tools/ca_vivaregress.py. ok=true: a natural correct answer — must score 100% (or, when 'hit' is given, must cover those key points). ok=false: a wrong answer — must score below 80% (not viva-ready) and must NOT cover the key points listed in 'miss'. Both matchers (Python tools/ca_vivamatch.py and JS js/ca-tools.js) are checked.

cases.a: Every transaction affects two accounts. One account gets debited and another gets credited by the same amount, so the total of debits always equals the total of credits and the trial balance can check the arithmetic.

It is the system where each transaction has a dual effect: an equal debit and credit is made in two accounts. Because of this, debits and credits always match, which helps in checking accuracy through a trial balance.

In double entry, for every debit there is a corresponding credit of equal value, since each transaction has two sides, giving and receiving. So the sum of all debits equals the sum of all credits, which proves arithmetical accuracy.
Double entry means each transaction is written twice in the journal so that there is a backup copy.
Under double entry both accounts are debited with the full amount.
Personal account: debit the receiver and credit the giver. Real account: debit what comes in, credit what goes out. Nominal account: debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains.

For personal accounts the receiver is debited and the giver is credited; for real accounts whatever comes into the business is debited and whatever goes out is credited; and for nominal accounts expenses and losses are debited while incomes and gains are credited.

Debit the receiver, credit the giver, that is for personal accounts. Debit what comes in and credit what goes out for real accounts. For nominal accounts, debit expenses and losses and credit income and gains.
Debit the giver and credit the receiver for personal accounts; debit what goes out and credit what comes in for real accounts; credit expenses and debit incomes for nominal accounts.
All three rules say debit the giver and credit the receiver.

Trade discount is never entered in the books; we record the transaction at the net price. Cash discount is recorded: the seller shows it as discount allowed, a loss, and the buyer shows it as discount received, a gain.

No entry is made for trade discount; goods are recorded at the invoice price after deducting it. Cash discount however is accounted for: the seller debits Discount Allowed Account and the buyer credits Discount Received Account.

Trade discount is simply deducted from the list price and not shown in the accounts, but cash discount is recorded, as Discount Allowed in the seller's books and as Discount Received in the buyer's books.
Both trade discount and cash discount are recorded in the books as discount allowed.
Trade discount is recorded as discount received by the seller, and cash discount is ignored.
Debit Drawings Account and credit Purchases Account with ₹5,000 at cost, because the owner receives the goods for personal use and the goods leave the business.
Drawings A/c Dr 5,000 To Purchases A/c 5,000. The goods are taken at cost price, not selling price, since the proprietor has withdrawn them for his own use, reducing his capital.
The entry is Drawings debit, Purchases credit, valued at the cost of five thousand rupees. Purchases are reduced because goods have gone out of the business to the owner, who is the receiver.
Debit Drawings and credit Sales with ₹5,000.
Debit Purchases and credit Drawings, because the goods return to stock.

Input tax is the GST we pay on purchases; it is debited to Input CGST and SGST accounts as an asset because it can be recovered. Output tax is the GST we collect on sales; it is credited as a liability payable to the government. Input tax is set off against output tax and only the net amount is paid. Note that CGST credit cannot be used for SGST, and SGST credit cannot be used for CGST.

GST paid when buying goods is input tax, a recoverable asset, so its account is debited. GST charged when selling is output tax, a liability, so it is credited. At the end of the month input is adjusted against output and the difference is paid. There is no cross-utilisation between CGST and SGST.

Input GST on purchases is debited and treated as an asset since we can claim it back; output GST on sales is credited and shown as a liability. We offset input against output and pay only the balance. Remember, CGST input cannot be used to pay SGST or the other way round.
Input tax is the GST collected on sales and is a liability; output tax is GST paid on purchases and is an asset.
Input tax and output tax are both credited and paid separately to the government; set-off is not allowed.

A ledger groups all the transactions relating to one account in one place, account-wise, whereas the journal records them in date order. It is the principal book because the trial balance and final accounts are drawn up from ledger balances.

The ledger is the book where every account is maintained separately, showing its full history; the journal is chronological. Since the financial statements are prepared from the ledger, it is called the principal book.

It is a classified record: the entries from the journal, which is kept date-wise, are sorted into individual accounts. The balances of these accounts go into the trial balance and then into the profit and loss account and balance sheet, so the ledger is the main book.
A ledger is a book where transactions are recorded in the order of their dates, before they go into the journal.
The ledger is called the principal book because cash is kept in it.

The account debited in the journal is posted on its debit side, with 'To' and the name of the account credited. The account credited is posted on its credit side with 'By' and the name of the account debited. The date, journal folio and amount are also written.

On the debit side of the account that was debited we write 'To' followed by the credited account's name; on the credit side of the account that was credited we write 'By' and the debited account's name, along with the date, the folio and the amount.

Post the debit in the journal to the debit side of that account, writing 'To' plus the name of the account credited; post the credit to the credit side of the other account, writing 'By' plus the name of the account debited. Each posting shows the date, J.F. and amount.
The account debited is posted on the credit side with 'By', and the account credited is posted on the debit side with 'To'.
Only the amount is posted, on whichever side has space.

Balancing means finding the difference between the two sides. Add up both sides, put the difference on the smaller side as 'Balance c/d' so that both totals are equal, and bring it down on the opposite side as 'Balance b/d' at the start of the next period.

We total the debit and credit sides, and the excess of the heavier side over the lighter side is entered on the lighter side as balance carried down. That same figure is then brought down on the other side as the opening balance for the next period.

First add both sides. The shortfall is written on the side with the lesser total as balance carried forward to make the two totals agree, and next period it appears on the opposite side as balance brought forward.
Balancing means making the debit side larger than the credit side by adding an extra entry.
The balance is written on the bigger side as balance brought down.
Personal and real accounts are balanced and carried forward to the next year, while nominal accounts are closed by transferring them to the Trading or Profit and Loss Account.

Accounts of persons, assets and liabilities, that is personal and real accounts, carry their balances into the next year. Expense and income accounts, the nominal ones, are not carried forward; they are transferred to the profit and loss account.

At the year end we close all nominal accounts to the Trading and Profit and Loss Account. Real and personal accounts are not closed; their balances are carried down to become next year's opening balances.
All accounts, including nominal accounts, are balanced and carried forward to next year.
Nominal accounts are carried forward and personal accounts are closed.

A debit balance means the debit side is bigger than the credit side; assets, expenses, losses and debtors usually show this. A credit balance means the credit side is bigger than the debit side; liabilities, capital, incomes, gains and creditors.

If the total of the debit side exceeds the credit side, the account has a debit balance, as with assets and expenses. If the credit side total is more, it has a credit balance, as with liabilities and incomes.
Debit balance: debits are more than credits, typical of assets, expenses and drawings. Credit balance: credits are more than debits, typical of capital, liabilities and income.
A debit balance shows the account has more credits than debits, like capital; a credit balance shows more debits, like assets.
Debit balance means a liability and credit balance means an asset.

A trial balance is a list of all ledger account balances on a given date. It is prepared to check the arithmetical accuracy of the books, to give a summary of the ledger, and to act as the basis for preparing final accounts.

It is a statement showing the debit and credit balances of every account on a particular day. Its purposes are to verify that posting and balancing are arithmetically correct, to provide a quick overview of the ledger, and to help prepare the financial statements.

A trial balance lists the totals or balances of the ledger accounts at a date. It helps detect arithmetical errors, summarises the whole ledger in one place and is the starting point for the profit and loss account and balance sheet.
A trial balance is the final statement of profit or loss for the year, showing whether the business made money.
It is a book of original entry where all cash transactions are recorded first.
The three methods are the total method, the balance method and the total-cum-balance method. The balance method is the one most commonly used because final accounts are prepared from balances.
A trial balance can be prepared by the totals method, the balances method or a combination of both. Most firms use the balances method since the final accounts need balances.
There is the total method, the balance method, and the compound method, which shows both totals and balances. In practice the balance method is the most popular.
The only method is the journal method, which lists every journal entry.
There are two methods, the journal method and the ledger method, and the ledger method is used most.
No. A tallied trial balance does not guarantee correct accounts, because errors of omission, errors of principle and compensating errors do not affect the agreement.

Not necessarily, it is not conclusive proof. For example, if a transaction is left out completely, or machinery is wrongly debited to purchases, which is an error of principle, the trial balance will still agree.

Agreement only shows arithmetical accuracy; it is not a proof that the books are free from errors. Compensating errors that cancel each other and posting to the wrong account on the correct side are not revealed.
Yes, if the trial balance agrees, the accounts are completely correct and free from all mistakes.
Yes, agreement proves that there are no errors of any kind.
A suspense account is a temporary account in which the difference in the trial balance is placed so that it agrees for now. It is closed once the errors are located and rectified.

When the trial balance does not tally and accounts must be finalised, the difference is put in a suspense account for the time being. As the errors are found and corrected, the suspense account balance becomes nil.
It is an interim account opened to carry the trial balance difference until the errors are traced. After all the errors are rectified, the suspense account disappears.
A suspense account is a permanent account for doubtful debts.
It is opened when the trial balance agrees, to record profits.
Sales returns go on the debit side, bank overdraft on the credit side, drawings on the debit side and outstanding expenses on the credit side.
Debit: sales returns and drawings. Credit: bank overdraft and outstanding expenses.
Returns inward is shown as a debit, bank overdraft is a liability shown as a credit, drawings are a debit balance and outstanding expenses are a credit, being a liability.
Sales returns go on the credit side because they are a gain.
All four items are shown in the profit and loss account, not in the trial balance.

Subsidiary books let the work be divided among several clerks, save time because only periodic totals are posted, make it easier to find errors, and give quick information like total credit sales for a month.

With separate books for purchases, sales, cash and returns, different people can keep different books at the same time. Posting is faster since only totals go to the ledger, mistakes can be traced easily, and management gets information readily.
They allow distribution of work among staff, speed up posting as only the monthly totals are posted, give better control and checking, and provide information such as monthly purchases at a glance.
Subsidiary books are kept only because the law requires a separate book for every customer.
They are kept so that every transaction is recorded twice for safety.

The purchases book records only credit purchases of goods meant for resale, at the net invoice amount after trade discount. Cash purchases go to the cash book, and credit purchases of assets like furniture go to the journal proper.

Only goods bought on credit for resale are entered there, from the suppliers' invoices, net of trade discount. Goods bought for cash are recorded in the cash book, and buying a machine on credit goes into the journal proper.

It is used for credit purchases of trading goods only, recorded at net amounts. It does not include cash purchases, which are in the cash book, or credit purchases of fixed assets, which are passed through the journal.
The purchases book records all purchases, cash and credit, including furniture and machinery.
It records cash purchases of goods, while credit purchases are kept in the sales book.

A debit note is sent by the buyer to the supplier when goods are returned, showing the supplier's account has been debited. A credit note is issued by the seller to the customer for goods returned, showing the customer's account has been credited. They are the basis of the purchase returns and sales returns books.

The buyer sends a debit note when he returns goods to the supplier; the seller issues a credit note when he accepts goods back from a customer. Debit notes support the returns outward book and credit notes support the returns inward book.
Debit note: prepared by the purchaser for purchase returns, debiting the supplier. Credit note: prepared by the seller for sales returns, crediting the customer.
A debit note is issued by the seller for goods returned by the customer, and a credit note is sent by the buyer to the supplier.
Debit note and credit note are the same document used for cash sales.
Each customer's account is debited separately with the invoice amount, and the total of the sales book is credited to Sales Account.
We debit every debtor individually and credit the periodical total to the Sales Account.
Individual customer accounts are debited with each sale, and at the end of the month the sales book total is credited to Sales Account.
The total of the sales book is debited to Sales Account and each customer is credited.
Only the grand total is posted, to Cash Account.

The journal proper is used for transactions that cannot be recorded in any other subsidiary book, such as opening entries, closing entries, adjustment entries, rectification of errors and goods lost by fire.
Entries that don't fit in the special books go there, for example the opening entry, depreciation and other adjustments, rectification entries, and purchase of furniture on credit.
Residual transactions which do not belong in any other book: opening and closing entries, transfer entries, credit purchase of machinery, goods withdrawn by the proprietor and loss by theft.
The journal proper records all cash sales and cash purchases.
It records credit sales of goods only.
Cash and bank transactions are recorded first in the cash book, so it is a book of original entry; it also replaces the cash account and bank account in the ledger, so it is a principal book.

Every cash receipt or payment is entered initially in the cash book. Because no separate cash account is opened in the ledger and the cash book itself serves as that account, it is a principal book as well.
It is where cash transactions are first written, and at the same time it acts as the Cash Account of the ledger, with its balance going directly to the trial balance.
The cash book is only a book of original entry; a separate Cash Account must still be kept in the ledger.
It is a principal book because it is kept by the principal cashier.

A contra entry is one that affects both cash and bank columns, like depositing cash into the bank. It appears on both sides of the cash book, is marked 'C' in the folio column, and is not posted to the ledger.

When cash is withdrawn from the bank for office use, both the cash and bank columns change; that is a contra entry. It is recorded on both sides, the letter C is written against it, and no posting is made in the ledger.

It is a transaction between the cash column and the bank column, such as paying cash into the bank. It is entered on the debit side and the credit side of the cash book, shown with a C in the L.F. column, and nothing is posted to the ledger.
A contra entry is a cash sale entered only in the cash column and posted to the Sales Account.
It is an entry that cancels another entry and is posted to the ledger on both sides.

Discount is not cash, so no money moves and there is nothing to balance. The discount allowed column on the debit side is totalled and debited to Discount Allowed Account, and the discount received column on the credit side is totalled and credited to Discount Received Account.

No actual cash is involved in a discount, so balancing has no meaning. The debit side discount total goes to Discount Allowed Account and the credit side discount total goes to Discount Received Account.

Discount columns are memorandum columns; they don't represent cash. The total of discount allowed on the receipts side is debited to Discount Allowed Account, and the total of discount received on the payments side is credited to Discount Received Account.
The discount columns are balanced like the cash column because discount is cash.
Discount allowed is on the credit side and discount received on the debit side.

The petty cashier is given a fixed amount at the beginning of the period. At the end, the main cashier reimburses exactly what was spent on the basis of vouchers, so the petty cashier starts again with the same fixed amount.
A definite sum called the imprest is advanced to the petty cashier; whatever he spends is refunded to him at the end of the week, restoring the full imprest.
Under the imprest system, a fixed float is handed to the petty cashier, and the amount used is topped up periodically so the balance returns to the original figure.
The petty cashier gets a different amount every month depending on what the manager decides.
Petty cash is the cash kept in the main cash book for big payments.
Debit Bank Account and credit Sales Account with the full ₹10,000. Then debit Commission Account and credit Bank Account with ₹200, which is 2% of the sale; the commission is a selling expense.
Sales of ₹10,000 are recorded at the full value: Bank Dr, Sales Cr. The bank's charge of ₹200 is booked separately as commission expense, Commission Dr, Bank Cr.
The seller records the sale gross: Bank Account is debited and Sales credited by ten thousand rupees, and then records commission of ₹200 as an expense by debiting Commission and crediting Bank.
Record the sale at ₹9,800 only, the net amount received from the bank.
Debit Bank ₹10,000 and credit Sales; the ₹200 commission is ignored.
Omission, commission, principle and compensating errors.

Errors can be errors of omission where an entry is left out, errors of commission like posting to the wrong account, errors of principle where capital and revenue items are confused, and compensating errors that offset each other.
The four types are: errors of omission, errors of commission, errors of principle and compensating errors.
The four errors are spelling errors, typing errors, printing errors and calculation errors.
There are errors of omission and casting errors only.

A one-sided error affects only one account, so the trial balance does not agree. A two-sided error affects two accounts equally, so the trial balance still agrees, and it is corrected by a journal entry.

In a one sided error just a single account is wrong, for instance the sales book is undercast, and this disturbs the trial balance. A two sided error involves two accounts, so the trial balance is not affected; it is rectified through a journal entry.

One-sided errors touch only one account and cause a difference in the trial balance; two-sided errors touch both accounts by the same amount, do not affect the agreement, and need a rectifying journal entry.
A one-sided error is an error in the bank statement and is ignored.
Both kinds of errors always make the trial balance disagree.
No journal entry is passed. We simply post the correction in the affected account on the required side, with a narration such as 'By under-casting of the sales book'.
Without passing any journal entry, the correct amount is entered directly in the account concerned, with an explanation like 'To undercasting of purchases book'.
It is corrected by a one-sided posting in that account only, not by a journal entry, and an explanatory note is written in the particulars.
Pass a journal entry debiting Suspense Account and crediting Sales Account.
Rectify it by reversing the whole original entry.

The trial balance difference is first put into a suspense account. One-sided errors found later are rectified through the suspense account, two-sided errors between the two accounts, and when all errors are corrected the suspense account is closed.
Suspense holds the difference temporarily. Each one sided error is corrected with suspense taking the other side of the entry, and after all corrections the suspense balance becomes zero.
It is opened with the amount of the difference; single-sided errors are corrected via the suspense account, and once every error is rectified it disappears.
Suspense account is used to record two-sided errors only, and it stays open permanently.
All errors are rectified through the suspense account, which then becomes the profit for the year.
This is an error of principle, since capital expenditure was treated as revenue. Debit Machinery Account and credit Wages Account with ₹9,000; profit goes up by ₹9,000 because the expense is reduced.
It is an error of principle. The correction is Machinery A/c Dr 9,000 To Wages A/c 9,000. As wages fall by ₹9,000, the profit increases by ₹9,000.
Error of principle: capital expenditure charged to revenue. Rectify by debiting Machinery and crediting Wages ₹9,000, which raises the profit by ₹9,000.
It is an error of omission; debit Wages and credit Machinery, and profit falls by ₹9,000.
Error of principle; debit Machinery, credit Wages; profit decreases by ₹9,000.
an agreement when enforceable by law can only become a contract, an agreement is not always a contract but a contract is always an agreement

An agreement is every promise or set of promises forming consideration for each other, basically offer plus acceptance, under Section 2(e). A contract is an agreement enforceable by law under Section 2(h). So a contract is always an agreement, but an agreement is not always a contract; for example, social agreements are not enforceable.
When an offer is accepted it becomes an agreement. If that agreement is enforceable by law, it becomes a contract. Hence all contracts are agreements but not all agreements are contracts.

Agreement means a promise made by accepting an offer; a contract is an agreement which the law will enforce. Every contract is an agreement, while an agreement need not be a contract, as a promise to go to a movie with a friend is not legally binding.
Every agreement is not a contract, but every contract is an agreement.
A contract is necessarily an agreement, whereas an agreement may not be a contract.
An agreement and a contract are the same thing; every agreement is a contract.
A contract is an offer, and an agreement is a contract enforceable by law; so an agreement is always a contract.
The parties must be competent to contract, their consent must be free, the consideration and the object must be lawful, and the agreement must not be one expressly declared void.
Competent parties, free consent, lawful consideration, lawful object, and not expressly declared to be void.
Under Section 10 there must be free consent of parties who have capacity to contract, a lawful consideration and a lawful purpose, and the agreement must not be one that the Act declares void.
A contract needs only an offer and acceptance in writing, signed by both parties.
The essentials are offer, acceptance and stamp duty.

An offer shows the willingness of a person to be bound, and once it is accepted a contract arises. An invitation to offer merely invites people to make offers, like a price list, a catalogue or goods displayed in a shop, as held in Pharmaceutical Society v Boots.
With an offer, acceptance creates a binding contract; an invitation to offer is just a step to start negotiations so that others can make offers. Advertisements and tenders are examples.

If I make an offer I am ready to be bound when you accept. A shop displaying goods with price tags is only inviting customers to offer to buy; the customer makes the offer at the counter, as in the Boots case.
An offer is any statement made by a seller, and once it is made the seller is bound.
Goods displayed in a shop window are an offer, so the shopkeeper must sell at that price.
No, silence cannot amount to acceptance. Acceptance has to be communicated, and the offeror cannot impose silence as acceptance, as decided in Felthouse v Bindley.
Mere silence is not acceptance; the acceptance must be expressed or conveyed to the offeror. In Felthouse versus Bindley the uncle said he would take silence as acceptance, but there was no contract.
Silence does not amount to acceptance because acceptance must be communicated to the proposer. This was laid down in Felthouse v. Bindley.
Yes, if the offeror says that silence will be treated as acceptance, silence binds the offeree.
Yes, silence is acceptance when the offer was made by post.

As against the proposer, communication of acceptance is complete when it is put in the course of transmission so that it is out of the acceptor's power. As against the acceptor, it is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer.
Against the offeror, acceptance is complete once the letter of acceptance is posted. Against the acceptor, it is complete only when the offeror learns of it.
For the proposer, the acceptance is complete as soon as it is sent and is beyond the acceptor's recall; for the acceptor, it is complete when the proposer receives it.
Acceptance is complete for both parties only when the proposer actually reads the letter.
As against the proposer it is complete when he receives the letter, and as against the acceptor when he posts it.
